analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 500 percent excise tax on corporate money spent on federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single member with no cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code to charge corporations a 500 percent excise tax on money they give to political committees and on electioneering communications, meaning every dollar of corporate election spending would trigger six dollars of cost. Corporations could not deduct that tax from their income taxes. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would face federal elections in which corporations could no longer flood campaigns with money, since the tax would make each dollar of corporate political spending cost six dollars. Candidates and campaigns funded by individuals rather than corporate treasuries would also operate on a more level field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary voters and candidates without corporate backing

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a tax equal to 500 percent of a corporation's contributions to political committees and its payments for electioneering communications, making corporate election spending prohibitively expensive. [S2][S3]
The bill denies corporations an income tax deduction for the excise tax, so corporations cannot pass the cost of the tax back to taxpayers through a write-off. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that spend money on federal campaigns and election advertising, which would bear a sixfold cost on every dollar of such spending, and indirectly the political committees and advertising channels that depend on corporate money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations spending money on federal elections

drawbacks.text: A 500 percent tax on corporate campaign spending functions as a near-prohibition on corporate political speech, and opponents argued after the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision that the First Amendment bars Congress from penalizing such spending; the bill anticipates this by disregarding any court determination that the campaign finance law does not apply to particular corporations. [S3]

The tax applies only to contributions and electioneering communications as defined by federal campaign finance law, so political money could shift toward channels the bill does not reach, such as other independent expenditures or nonprofit groups that do not disclose their donors. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: the bill would sharply reduce corporate money in federal elections, but it would do so with a punitive tax that courts would very likely strike down, and it could push political money into less transparent channels rather than out of politics. As drafted, it is more a statement of principle than a workable law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the bill on March 13, 2013. [S1][S5]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction. [S5]
No hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died at the end of the 113th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and their political committees, which kept spending on federal elections without facing any new tax, are better off because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill imposing a 500 percent excise tax on corporate campaign contributions and electioneering communications.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Chair Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As the member who controlled the committee's agenda, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill alone and no Republican cosponsored it; with a Republican majority controlling Ways and Means, the bill went nowhere, so support and opposition fell entirely along party lines. [S4][S5]

industries.industry: Corporations that spend on federal campaigns and election advertising
industries.note: These companies would pay a sixfold cost on every dollar of political spending, which the bill's premise holds is spent to shape tax, regulatory, and contract policy in their favor. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against voters' interest in elections not dominated by corporate treasuries. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Political committees, campaign consultants, and election advertising media
industries.note: Groups that receive and spend corporate money and firms that sell election advertising would see a major funding source taxed away. Their interest in the bill is mixed: they depend on the money, but the tax targets only its corporate portion. [S3]
